# Diagnosing Intermittent Fuel Cutoff on Royal Enfield Classic

A motorcycle that runs for a few kilometers and then dies is a classic symptom of a failing fuel delivery system or an electrical interruption in the ignition path. In your specific case, the Royal Enfield 350 Classic has exhibited this behavior repeatedly despite multiple interventions. The diagnostic journey you describedâmoving from a suspected water contamination to rust accumulation on the petroloff switch and finally to a vague "engine problem"âfollows a logical troubleshooting path common in older carbureted engines.

The most immediate suspect is the fuel delivery chain, specifically how contaminants interact with the mechanical components of the carburetor and the ignition switch. When you replaced the petrol off switch due to rust, you addressed a potential electrical contact issue. However, if the tank itself harbors significant internal corrosion or sediment, simply cleaning it once is often insufficient. Rust flakes act like sandpaper; they can clog the narrow jets of a carburetor or accumulate in the float bowl, eventually blocking fuel flow entirely after a certain distance traveled. This explains why the bike runs for 2 to 3 kilometers (consuming the cleaner fuel near the bottom of the tank) before shutting down when the pickup valve encounters debris or air pockets created by uneven sediment distribution.

If the mechanical cleaning and switch replacement did not resolve the issue, you must look at the fuel pump mechanism found in modern Royal Enfield Classics. The 350 Classic utilizes an electric fuel pump located under the seat. A common failure mode here is a clogged filter screen or a failing pump diaphragm. When the bike sits for extended periods, fuel degrades and can leave varnish-like deposits that adhere to these components. Over time, as you ride and the fuel level drops, these deposits can shift, causing an intermittent blockage. The "engine problem" diagnosis from the showroom likely refers to the engine cutting off due to lack of fuel reaching the carburetor jets, rather than a mechanical failure within the combustion chamber itself.

To systematically resolve this, consider performing a bench test on the fuel pump. Disconnect the fuel line at the tank outlet and run the ignition switch to "on" while observing the flow rate directly into a container. If the flow is weak or stops intermittently, the pump is likely failing internally. Additionally, verify that the fuel filter (often integrated into the pump assembly) has not become saturated with particulate matter despite previous cleaning attempts.

Another critical area to investigate is the carburetor jetting and needle valve. Rust particles from the tank can physically lodge in the main jet or the pilot jet. Even after flushing the tank, if a small fragment remains lodged in the fuel line leading to the carburetor, it will cause an air-lock effect once the engine reaches a specific RPM or fuel temperature, mimicking a complete shutdown.

If you have already replaced the switch and cleaned the tank multiple times without success, the next step is to replace the entire fuel pump assembly along with the filter screen. This ensures that any internal wear or micro-fractures in the old pump are eliminated. Finally, inspect the fuel lines for kinks or hardening, which can restrict flow under vibration. Addressing these specific points should restore consistent fuel delivery and eliminate the intermittent stalling.
